entries.value:
A file reopened from the archive (12 March 1994, closed as an ‘accident’):

· Lola Reyes (19) died in a fall down the back stairs of the Tablao La Cava. Sole eyewitness: guitarist Rafael Montoya — ‘I saw her fall.’
· Statement of the costumier Pilar Ruiz: ‘I didn’t see anything.’ Nobody asked her what she heard.
· Autopsy note, disregarded at the time: ‘Bruising on the breastbone the size of two palms.’
· Lola Reyes’s draft contract: with a Madrid company; her contract with the owner, Joaquín Ortega, was due to end a week later.
A closed file, back on the desk thirty-six years later.

· Cause of death: strangulation with a thin steel wire; a mark fully encircling the neck, crossed at the back.
· Under the nails, not skin but black leather fibres: the attacker was wearing gloves.
· The victim was seated; the attack came from behind, by someone standing.
· Time of death: 00.30–01.10.
The door of the safe in the office creaks.
The show ends; the dancer goes down to the bar.
The owner goes upstairs with gloves in his hand.
I sing; God knows the rest.
After the show we always have a glass together. Rafael didn’t come. I went up; he was sitting in his chair, his head dropped on his chest. His guitar was in his lap. The coil of string on the floor.
He buttons and unbuttons his jacket.

Lola. Lola Reyes, 1994. Nineteen years old, the best this tablao ever had. She fell down these stairs, they said. Rafael gave a statement that night: ‘I saw her fall.’ For thirty-six years he kept quiet. Last month he told me, ‘Curro, I didn’t see her fall; I saw her pushed.’
What was Rafael talking about these last few days?
Where did the killer’s gloves go?
There were no gloves in the costume room.
The gloves hadn’t been thrown into the river.
It was recorded that the gloves were found in Joaquín Ortega’s safe.
Curro Amaya was taken into custody; Lola Reyes’s name was forgotten once more.
Joaquín Ortega was arrested; the 1994 file was reopened as ‘murder’. The Fundación Santa Ana grants landed on the Triana branch’s desk.
Pilar Ruiz was taken into custody; the tablao opened again the next evening.
Macarena Flores was arrested; the 1994 file stayed in the archive.
The cantaor found the body and told of the victim’s 1994 confession; he wasn’t the one who went upstairs with gloves.

His gloves were found in his safe, with wire cuts and the victim’s blood on the palms; the student saw him go upstairs with the gloves. The 1994 file shows why the victim withdrawing his statement would ruin him.
At that hour the costumier was sewing the student’s skirt.
The dancer argued with the victim, but after the show she was in front of the barman until two.
This tablao is forty years old; gossip won’t bring it down.
Lola fell. I was at the top of the stairs, yes; whether I caught her or pushed her, for thirty-six years I haven’t known.

Rafael said, ‘On Monday I’ll go with my daughter and tell them.’ Lola, me, the foundation’s money, all of it. I took my gloves and went upstairs; the same stairs I always climb. I unwound the string from its coil. I put the gloves in the safe. I weep for Lola every night too, believe me.
In my office, with the accounts. I didn’t go upstairs. Rafael and I are friends of forty years; Lola’s death broke us both.
He turns the rings on his fingers.
Where were you after the show?
1994 is closed. An accident. Rafael got old; he got confused.
I’m a student here; I don’t really know anyone.

In the costume room, with Ms Pilar, having my skirt sewn. The costume room door looks onto the stairs. After half past twelve Mr Joaquín went upstairs, to the dressing room. He had gloves in his hand, black; he wasn’t wearing them, he was carrying them. Ten minutes later he came down. Now I remember the gloves, but at the time I thought, ‘Is it cold, maybe?’
She tucks her hair behind her ear.
Where were you after the show?

Macarena came straight down and sat in front of me until two. Curro and Ms Pilar for a while. Mr Joaquín didn’t stop by the bar; a little after half twelve I heard him open the safe in his office — the safe door creaks.
He throws the bar cloth over his shoulder.
Who was at the bar after the show?
Someone in gloves strangled him from behind with a guitar string
If we’re talking about my father, I speak as his daughter, not as a lawyer.

He showed me a draft: a petition withdrawing his 1994 statement. ‘You hand it in, my girl,’ he said. We were going to hand it in on Monday. He’d told Joaquín too; ‘I owed it to him to say it to his face,’ he said. That was my father.
She straightens the lapel of her blazer.
What was your father doing these last few days?
In Triana a tablao’s guitarist was strangled with his own string in the dressing room. In 1994 a dancer died on the same stairs.
58, cantaor; the victim’s friend of thirty years.
31, a Turkish flamenco student; works at the tablao.
71, the tablao’s costumier; she was there in 1994 too.

Lola told Joaquín, ‘I’m signing with Madrid, not with you.’ That night they were shouting at the top of the stairs. I was downstairs; I heard the voices, then a crash. They took my statement; I said ‘I didn’t see anything.’ I hadn’t seen. But I had heard. Nobody asked.
I sew fabric, and I sew my mouth shut.
Every night. I sewed Elif’s skirt. Who went up the stairs and who came down, I don’t look any more. I learned not to look in 1994.
She turns the thimble on her finger.
Were you in the costume room last night?

On the night of 15 October 2030, at the Tablao La Cava in Triana, the guitarist Rafael Montoya (61) was found dead after the show in the upstairs dressing room. The mark of a steel guitar string on his neck.

The cantaor Curro Amaya found the body at 01.20. In the tablao that night: owner Joaquín Ortega, dancer Macarena Flores, costumier Pilar Ruiz, barman Mateo Santos, flamenco student Elif Kaya. The victim’s daughter Inés Montoya arrived in the morning.
Request permission to open the 1994 file from the archive
Request permission to open Joaquín Ortega’s safe

The safe in Joaquín Ortega’s office (with the branch chief’s approval):

· A pair of thin black leather gloves; steel wire cuts and the victim’s blood on the palms. The glove fibres match those under the victim’s nails.
· €1.1 million from the Fundación Santa Ana over the last fifteen years under the name ‘cultural grant’; on every payment document the ‘adviser approval’ box is ticked.
· A photocopy of Rafael Montoya’s draft petition; in the margin, in Joaquín Ortega’s handwriting: ‘Monday.’

The cantaor told of the confession, the daughter of the petition, the costumier of what she heard in 1994; those three got the archive opened. The student saw the man with gloves on the stairs, the barman heard the creak of the safe. The search gave the gloves and the foundation’s grant.
In Sevilla old files don’t close; they just wait.

In 1994 the dancer Lola Reyes, about to leave the owner Joaquín Ortega for Madrid, fell down the tablao’s stairs; the guitarist Rafael Montoya said ‘I saw her fall’. Thirty-six years later Rafael decided to withdraw his statement and to say so to Joaquín’s face. After the show Joaquín went upstairs with his gloves, strangled Rafael with his own guitar string and put the gloves in his safe.
I dance; I don’t know what’s beyond the stage.
He dropped the tempo again, and I said so in front of everyone. On stage we fight, then we kiss; that’s flamenco. After the show I went straight down to the bar; ask Mateo.
She adjusts the carnation in her hair.
You argued with Rafael before the show.
A half-unwound coil of steel guitar string; flecks of leather at both ends.
A yellowed cardboard folder; inside, a photograph of a staircase and a one-page statement.
Gloves from inside a safe, with fine steel marks on the palms.
